benefits: Compares completely different investments on one fair scale.
The annualized figure stops a 3-year 35% gain from looking better than a 1-year 20% gain.
Shows whether an investment actually beat inflation and fees, not just its purchase price.
Free, instant, and private - no brokerage login needed.

faqs.a: For a single lump-sum investment, annualized return and CAGR are the same thing: the steady yearly rate that would grow the start value to the end value. ROI is the total gain; CAGR is that gain expressed as a per-year rate.
faqs.q: What is the difference between ROI and CAGR?

faqs.a: Total ROI ignores time, which is exactly why it misleads. A 50% gain over 10 years is only about 4.1% per year - less than many savings accounts pay. Always look at the annualized return when comparing investments held for different periods.

Subtract all costs - brokerage fees, taxes, and any maintenance - from the final value first, then run the calculation. Fees quietly eat several percentage points off the headline ROI of actively managed investments.
faqs.q: How do I include fees in ROI?

faqs.a: It can be. An ROI of -30% simply means you lost 30% of what you put in. The annualized figure works the same way: if your $10,000 fell to $7,000 in 3 years, ROI is -30% and the annualized return is about -11.3% per year.
Basic ROI assumes one amount in and one amount out. If you added or removed money along the way, use an IRR or XIRR calculation instead - most spreadsheet apps have one built in.
faqs.q: What if I added money during the investment?

faqs.a: No. ROI tells you how much money grew, not how much risk you took to grow it. A 15% ROI from a calm index fund and a 15% ROI from a volatile crypto bet are very different propositions - risk-adjusted measures like the Sharpe ratio handle that question.

roi-calculator.formula:
ROI = (final value - initial cost) / initial cost x 100.
Annualized return = (final / initial)^(1 / years) - 1, expressed as a percent.
Multiple = final / initial (e.g. 1.35x).
howTo: Enter the total amount you originally invested, including any purchase fees.
Enter the current or sale value of the investment.
Enter how many years you held it (fractions are fine, e.g. 1.5).
Read the total ROI, the annualized return, the gain in dollars, and the multiple.
Compare the annualized return against inflation and alternative investments.
keyFacts: ROI = return on investment = (gain) / (cost), usually expressed as a percentage.
It measures total profit relative to what you paid, ignoring how long it took.
Annualized return (CAGR) converts the gain into an equivalent yearly rate for fair comparisons.
A positive ROI means you made money; a negative ROI means you lost money.
ROI alone does not account for risk, taxes, or the time value of money.

limitations: Ignores taxes and fees unless you subtract them from the final value yourself.
Does not handle deposits or withdrawals made during the holding period.
Says nothing about the risk taken to earn the return.
A single past ROI never guarantees future results.

roi-calculator.quickAnswer: ROI (return on investment) is your profit divided by what you paid, as a percentage: (final value - initial cost) / initial cost x 100. For example, $10,000 growing to $13,500 over 3 years is a 35% ROI, but the annualized return is only about 10.52% per year - the steady yearly rate that would produce the same result. Always compare the annualized figure when investments were held for different lengths of time.
roi-calculator.tagline: Find your return on investment percentage, annualized return, and total gain.
roi-calculator.workedExample:
Invest $10,000, sell for $13,500 after 3 years:
1. Gain = 13,500 - 10,000 = $3,500.
2. ROI = 3,500 / 10,000 x 100 = 35%.
3. Multiple = 13,500 / 10,000 = 1.35x.
4. Annualized = 1.35^(1/3) - 1 = 0.1052 = 10.52% per year.
So the headline is 35%, but the fair yearly comparison figure is 10.52%.
